title: Abu Bakr's inaugural
hook: I'm not the best of you: help me if I do right, correct me if I do wrong
tomorrow: two friends, one argument, and you're the judge. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell sermon, read whole: all from Adam. Then the Prophet died, and someone had to stand up next.

Red ink across an essay stings, even when every mark is right. The scratch of the pen, the circled word, the note in the margin. Plenty of us hand in our work hoping for a clean page. When Abu Bakr stood up as leader after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he did something else on his first day. He handed the people the red pen, and asked them to use it on him.
screen: `THE SCRATCH OF A RED PEN.` → `HOPING FOR A CLEAN PAGE.` → `HE HANDED OVER THE PEN.`

segments.voice: The speech is kept in Ibn Hisham's edition of Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet. Abu Bakr says: I have been given authority over you, and I am not the best of you. If I do well, help me. If I do wrong, set me right. Truthfulness is a trust, and lying is a betrayal. The weak among you is strong in my eyes until I secure his right, and the strong among you is weak in my eyes until I take from him what he owes. Obey me as long as I obey God and his Messenger; if I disobey, you owe me no obedience. Hear what he's doing. No plan, no boast. He names the limit of his own power, out loud, before anyone asks. His Arabic for set me right is qawwimuni: straighten me, the way you'd straighten something bent. Feel the weight of that picture in your hand: a crooked stick, held and pressed until it runs true. He expects to bend. He asks the crowd to do the pressing. Being corrected still stings. He asked for it anyway, at the very start, and named the people he'd protect: the weak, until they had their right.
screen: `NOT THE BEST OF YOU.` · `HELP ME, OR SET ME RIGHT.` · `THE WEAK STRONG, THE STRONG WEAK.` · `QAWWIMUNI: STRAIGHTEN ME.` · then, large: `CORRECT ME.`

segments.voice: Hold out one open hand, palm up, as if offering someone your pen. Let the arm rest, and keep the hand open. With each breath out, say inside: correct me. When the words start to feel uncomfortable, keep the hand open anyway.
Abu Bakr's inaugural: his speech on taking office, asking the people to help him when right and set him straight when wrong.
Carry this: correct me, said out loud before anyone has to say it to you. Day 1642, straightened.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers retell Abu Bakr's speech when they speak about leadership, accountability and consultation, often alongside the Qur'an's call to take counsel together.

fork.setup: you're the new shift lead at the coffee shop. on day one, which sentence fits Abu Bakr?
options: if I get something wrong, tell me. I'd rather know.
I've got this, so trust me and don't second-guess.
let's vote on everything, so nobody has to lead.
fork.reveal: he led, and still asked to be set right: help me if I do well, correct me if I do wrong.

original.note: Arabic: qawwimuni, straighten me, set me right: Abu Bakr's word in the speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: a new leader should look certain.
what it means: Abu Bakr asked for help when right and correction when wrong, and set limits on his own power.
what a scholar hears: the speech in Ibn Hisham's edition of Ibn Ishaq's Sira; qawwimuni, straighten me, from the verb for setting something upright.

his last words to the companions before he died

chat.says: advisor made me lead of the tutoring club. first meeting tomorrow. how do i not sound like a dictator
options: Ask them to tell you when you're wrong, and mean it. Abu Bakr opened with exactly that.
Show you're the best choice right away, so nobody doubts you when you make calls.
Let everyone decide everything. A good leader doesn't really make calls at all.

notes: Abu Bakr's address paraphrased (Guillaume's English is not public domain). Lines: not the best of you; help me / set me right (qawwimuni); truthfulness a trust (amana), lying treachery (khiyana); weak strong / strong weak; obey me while I obey God. Confirm wording and that 'qawwimuni' is the form in Ibn Hisham.

'Straighten me, the way you'd straighten something bent' is a plain reading of the verb (q-w-m, form II: to set upright); the crooked-stick picture is the mascot's image, not a claim about the text. Confirm.
